prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current robotic manipulation systems rely heavily on visual affordances and internalized common sense to interact with objects. While this works for simple tools (e.g., hammers), it fails for complex electrical appliances where form does not strictly dictate function (e.g., distinguishing a "temperature" knob from a "timer" knob on a microwave). The functional semantics of these appliances are defined by manufacturers and encapsulated in user manuals, not in the object's geometry. Existing research faces a critical gap: there are no benchmarks or datasets that align multi-page, multi-modal user manuals with 3D articulated object models suitable for robotic simulation. Consequently, robots remain unable to consult documentation to solve novel, long-horizon manipulation tasks.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that a robot can successfully manipulate unseen, complex appliances by treating user manuals as a primary observation modality alongside vision. Specifically, we posit that by grounding the semantic information extracted from instruction manuals (text and diagrams) onto the physical visual observation of the appliance, an agent can infer correct interaction sequences without prior specific training on that device. We further believe that we can overcome the data scarcity in this domain by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to synthesize realistic, consistent user manuals directly from articulated CAD assets.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a two-fold approach: creating a simulation benchmark and developing a planning architecture capable of reading manuals.

**1. Synthetic Manual Generation Pipeline (Data Engine)**
To create a large-scale training and evaluation benchmark, we will design a semi-automated pipeline to generate realistic manuals for existing 3D CAD datasets.
*   **Semantic Annotation:** We will employ Multimodal LLMs to analyze CAD models and assign functional names and state transitions to manipulable parts (e.g., assigning a knob as "Timer" with specific rotation limits).
*   **Task & Content Generation:** The LLM will generate logical manipulation tasks (e.g., "Defrost bread") and the corresponding step-by-step instructions.
*   **Visual Synthesis:** We will procedurally render "instructional diagrams" (e.g., control panel close-ups, motion arrows) and combine them with the text using automated document compilation to produce realistic PDF manuals.

**2. Manual-Driven Planning Framework (The Agent)**
We plan to develop a modular architecture, "ManualPlan," designed to translate document instructions into physical actions.
*   **Manual Resolution Module:** This module will ingest PDF documents, parsing them into text and visual elements (figures/tables) to create a searchable knowledge base of the appliance's functions.
*   **Visual Grounding & Part Alignment:** A core challenge is linking the manual's diagram to the robot's live camera feed. We will utilize a visual prompting strategy (Set-of-Mark) where the live observation is segmented and overlaid with unique markers. An MLLM will then reason over the marked image and the manual to map functional labels (from the text) to specific physical parts (masks) in the scene.
*   **Hierarchical Planning:** An LLM planner will decompose the high-level task into a sequence of primitive actions based on the manual's instructions. These plans will drive either a library of geometric primitives (if CAD poses are known) or an open-vocabulary manipulation policy (if operating vision-only) to execute the movements.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Foundational Benchmark:** The creation of the first dataset aligning diverse appliance CAD models with full, multi-page user manuals and manipulation tasks, enabling quantitative evaluation of manual-guided robotics.
*   **Novel Task Formulation:** Defining a new class of manipulation challenges that require cross-modal reasoning between document understanding and physical interaction.
*   **Baseline Architecture:** A proposed framework for grounding technical documentation into robotic action, demonstrating how general-purpose MLLMs can be leveraged to solve the "instruction-following" problem for complex machinery.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a benchmark and evaluation protocol to test robotic manipulation of appliances using user manuals.

*   **Datasets:** "CheckManual" Dataset.
    *   **Source:** Appliance CAD models collected from PartNet-Mobility Dataset.
    *   **Scale:** 369 appliances across 11 categories (including washing machines, coffee makers, dishwashers, microwaves, ovens, cameras, displays, printers, fridges, blenders).
    *   **Manuals:** 1107 generated manuals (PDF format).
    *   **Components:** 2211 manipulable parts (buttons, knobs, levers, sliders, doors, lids, containers). Average of 6.00 manipulable parts per appliance.
    *   **Tasks:** 1464 manipulation tasks (short-horizon and long-horizon, max 18 steps). Average of 1.32 tasks per manual.
    *   **Data Generation:** Used a large model-assisted pipeline (GPT-4o) with human verification for function name annotation, state annotation, and task creation.

*   **Evaluation Tracks:**
    *   **Track 1: Manual-CAD-Appliance Aligned Planning.**
        *   **Inputs:** Task Instruction, RGB-D Observation, Manual PDF, Appliance CAD Model.
        *   **Goal:** High-level Planning (align manual function names to parts; plan manipulation steps).
        *   **Note:** Free from physical manipulation execution.
    *   **Track 2: Manual & CAD based Manipulation.**
        *   **Inputs:** Task Instruction, RGB-D Observation, Manual PDF, Appliance CAD Model.
        *   **Goal:** Low-level Manipulation execution (using two-finger gripper).
        *   **Constraint:** Mapping relationships between manual, CAD, and observation are unknown.
    *   **Track 3: Pure Manual-based Manipulation.**
        *   **Inputs:** Task Instruction, RGB-D Observation, Manual PDF.
        *   **Goal:** Low-level Manipulation execution.
        *   **Constraint:** No CAD model assistance. Relies solely on RGB-D and manual.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Track 1:**
        *   **Part Alignment Success Rate:** Confirmed when all CAD model parts were linked to correct function names in the manual.
        *   **Task Planning Success Rate:** Confirmed when part IDs and actions in every planned step were correct.
    *   **Track 2 & 3:**
        *   **Task Success Rate:** All steps completed in correct order.
        *   **Task Completion Rate:** Calculated as (Number of Success Steps / Number of Total Task Steps). Only steps before the first failure counted.
    *   **Physical Success Criteria (Simulation):**
        *   Revolute parts (knobs/levers/doors): Acceptable error range defined as Limit $\pm 30^\circ$.
        *   Prismatic parts (buttons/sliders): Success when movement $> 25\%$ of Limit or if (Motion Distance Part / Motion Distance Appliance) $> 50\%$ (if target and appliance move in same direction).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **ManualPlan (Track 1):** A proposed framework utilizing OCR (Paddle OCR), MLLM (GPT-4o) for manual resolution, and LLM for planning. Uses Grounding-DINO and SAM for part alignment (Set-of-Mark prompting).
    *   **ManualPlan + Primitive Actions (Track 2):** Uses ManualPlan for high-level planning. Uses FoundationPose for 6-DoF pose estimation to align observed appliance with CAD. Executes using CAD-assisted primitive actions.
    *   **ManualPlan + VoxPoser (Track 3):** Integrates ManualPlan with the open-vocabulary manipulation model VoxPoser for CAD-free execution.
    *   **Ablation (All Tracks):** "w/o manual" (Inputting only task instruction and observation, removing the manual PDF).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Simulation Environment:** SAPIEN.
    *   **Robot:** Franka Panda with flying gripper.
    *   **Sensors:** Simulated RealSense D415 RGB-D camera.
    *   **Models:** GPT-4o (Large Language Model & Multimodal Large Language Model), Grounding-DINO (Object Detection), Segment Anything (SAM - Segmentation), FoundationPose (Pose Estimation), Paddle OCR (Text Extraction).
    *   **Real Robot Setup:** Franka Panda arm with RealSense D415 mounted on end-effector.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Impact of Manuals (Visual Observation):** Without a manual, robots lacked knowledge of concrete functions (e.g., distinguishing temperature vs. time knobs on a microwave). With the manual, the robot could align visual features (like specific buttons) with functions described in the text to execute tasks like "Open the Door."
*   **Part Distribution:** Buttons were the most frequent component type (approx. 1210), followed significantly by knobs (approx. 562), then doors (approx. 177). Other components like sliders, lids, lenses, containers, levers, portafilters, slots, shelves, and screens appeared less frequently.
*   **Task Complexity:** Manipulation tasks typically ranged from 1 to 18 steps. The frequency peaked at 1-step tasks and 3-step tasks, with a long tail extending to complex 18-step tasks.
*   **Performance Analysis (Track 1):** While ManualPlan could generate correct task plans, MLLMs struggled with the "Part Alignment" phase—specifically mapping manual part annotations to the corresponding appliance CAD models or visual observations.
*   **Performance Analysis (Tracks 2 & 3):** Performance dropped significantly compared to planning. We attributed this to error accumulation over long-horizon tasks. A failure in part identification, planning, or a single execution step caused the entire task to fail.
*   **Ablation Study:** Removing the manual ("w/o manual") resulted in significantly lower success rates across all tracks, confirming the necessity of the manual for comprehending specific appliance functions that are not inferable from common sense alone.
*   **Real World Deployment:** We successfully deployed the Track 3 setting (Pure Manual-based) on a physical Franka Panda robot. The system was able to open a microwave door by reading the manual, though we noted the need to cache correct actions to mitigate error accumulation in long sequences.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

```

    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
While robotic manipulation has advanced significantly for simple tools, electrical appliances present a unique challenge: their functionality cannot be inferred solely from visual appearance or general common sense. For instance, visually identical buttons on a microwave may control vastly different functions (e.g., temperature vs. timer), and specific operational sequences are required by manufacturers. Humans rely on user manuals to bridge this gap, yet current robotic systems lack the capability to comprehend multi-page documents and translate them into physical actions.

Existing research in this domain is bifurcated and insufficient. Manipulation models can handle simple tools but fail to read manuals. Conversely, "manual-related" datasets are restricted to Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks like Question Answering (QA) and lack the 3D CAD models required for physical simulation and manipulation training. There is currently no framework that aligns appliance manuals with 3D articulated models to enable comprehensive manual-based robotic manipulation.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that by synthesizing a large-scale, aligned dataset of appliance CAD models and procedurally generated user manuals, we can train and evaluate agents on "Manual-based Appliance Manipulation."

Our core hypothesis is that a hierarchical planning framework, which we call **ManualPlan**, can solve long-horizon manipulation tasks by treating the manual as an external knowledge base. By utilizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for high-level reasoning and a "Set-of-Mark" (SoM) visual prompting mechanism for grounding, the system will effectively align 2D manual diagrams with 3D real-world observations. This will allow a robot to infer function-to-part mappings and execute complex instruction sequences without prior training on the specific appliance instance.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a comprehensive project consisting of two main pillars: the **CheckManual Benchmark** (a data generation pipeline) and the **ManualPlan Model** (an algorithmic framework).

### 1. The CheckManual Data Generation Pipeline
We will develop a semi-automated pipeline to generate high-quality, diverse appliance manuals linked to articulated CAD models (sourced from datasets like PartNet-Mobility). This pipeline will leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate LaTeX code, ensuring standardized yet flexible document creation.

**A. Functional Annotation & State Definition**
We will employ MLLMs to annotate the functions of manipulable parts on CAD models.
1.  **Point-Line Annotation:** We will identify manipulable parts and use MLLMs to assign function names (e.g., "Temperature Knob") based on visual features.
2.  **State Sampling:** We will algorithmically sample function states based on part types:
    *   **Buttons:** Random push times within a range.
    *   **Knobs/Levers:** Random rotation degrees at intervals of $60^{\circ}$.
    *   **Doors/Lids:** Binary states ("Open"/"Close").

**B. Figure & Layout Generation**
To mimic real-world manuals, we will generate specific visual assets:
*   **Cover Images:** We will use the SDXL-Lightning text-to-image model to synthesize appliance overviews within context-appropriate backgrounds (e.g., kitchens for ovens).
*   **Control Panels:** We will apply the **DBSCAN** clustering algorithm to geometrical centers of buttons/knobs. If clusters are found, we generate close-up "Control Panel" diagrams using edge detection for sketch-style rendering.
*   **Manipulation Guidance:** We will generate diagrams visualizing interaction physics (trajectory lines, motion decomposition) by calculating the motion trajectory of contact points relative to the part-linked joint axis.

**C. LaTeX Compilation**
We will design a modular LaTeX generation system where an LLM generates code sections sequentially. The system will compile these into PDF format, incorporating the generated figures and task descriptions (e.g., tables, bullet lists).

### 2. The ManualPlan Architecture
We will develop a baseline model, **ManualPlan**, designed to operate in three challenge tracks: (1) Alignment/Planning, (2) CAD-Assisted Manipulation, and (3) Pure Manual-based Manipulation.

**Phase 1: Manual Resolution**
We will parse the PDF manuals by converting pages to images. We will utilize **PaddleOCR** for text extraction and an MLLM to detect visual elements (figures, tables). This yields a structured representation of the manual's content.

**Phase 2: Part Alignment via Set-of-Mark (SoM)**
To map manual instructions to the physical robot observation, we will implement a visual prompting mechanism:
1.  **Detection:** We will use **Grounding-DINO** to predict bounding boxes of movable parts in the robot's view.
2.  **Segmentation:** These boxes will prompt the **Segment Anything Model (SAM)** to generate masks.
3.  **Visual Prompting:** We will overlay these masks with unique numeric IDs and semi-transparent colors onto the observation image.
4.  **Alignment:** An MLLM will take this "marked" image and the manual diagrams as input to output the mapping between Mask IDs and Manual Function Names.

**Phase 3: Manipulation Planning**
An LLM will act as the high-level planner. Given a task instruction $T$, it will output a sequence of steps. Each step must define the target part and the specific state change in a dictionary format:
$$ \text{Step}_i = \{ \text{'PartName'}: \text{'TargetState'} \} $$
Example: `{'Brew Strength Lever': 'Rotate 60 degrees'}`.

**Phase 4: Low-Level Execution Policies**
We will implement two distinct execution strategies:

*   **CAD-Assisted Policy (Track 2):**
    We will estimate the 6-DoF pose of the appliance. We define primitive actions based on part geometry:
    *   *Buttons:* Push vector is the normal direction of the surface geometric center.
    *   *Knobs:* Grasp pose is aligned with the normal of the surface center; execution involves rotating the gripper by the planned degrees.
    *   *Doors/Sliders:* We will constrain the **AnyGrasp** model using the part's 3D bounding box to predict grasp poses.

*   **CAD-Free Policy (Track 3):**
    We will integrate the **VoxPoser** open-vocabulary model. ManualPlan will function as the high-level "cerebrum" providing natural language constraints, while VoxPoser acts as the "cerebellum," generating 3D value maps to guide the end-effector based on the RGB-D observation.

### 3. Evaluation Metrics Definition
We will define strict success criteria for physical manipulation. Let $L$ be the whole movement limitation range of a target joint.

For **revolute parts** (knobs, doors), a step is successful if the error is within a threshold:
$$ \text{Success}_{\text{revolute}} \iff | \theta_{\text{final}} - \theta_{\text{target}} | \le 30^{\circ} $$
where the acceptable range is defined as $L \pm 30^{\circ}$.

For **prismatic parts** (sliders, buttons), success requires substantial movement relative to the total range or appliance motion:
$$ \text{Success}_{\text{prismatic}} \iff (\Delta d > 0.25 \times L) \lor \left( \frac{MD_{\text{part}}}{MD_{\text{appliance}}} > 0.5 \right) $$
where $MD$ represents motion distance, ensuring the part moves significantly more than the appliance base itself.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **First Manual-Centric Benchmark:** We will provide the research community with the first dataset aligning PDF manuals, structured tasks, and 3D articulated CAD models, enabling rigorous evaluation of document-grounded manipulation.
2.  **Novel Grounding Framework:** The ManualPlan architecture will demonstrate how Set-of-Mark visual prompting can bridge the domain gap between schematic technical documents and real-world visual observations.
3.  **Holistic Manipulation Pipeline:** By integrating high-level reasoning with low-level primitives (and open-vocabulary controllers like VoxPoser), we aim to establish a baseline for robots that can walk up to a novel appliance, read the manual, and operate it successfully.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
